question: Who built the pyramids of Giza?

passages.title: Who Built the Pyramids? | NOVA | PBS
passages.text: Who Built the Pyramids? Egyptologists and historians have long debated the question of who built the Pyramids, and how. Standing at the base of the Pyramids at Giza it is hard to believe that any of these enormous monuments could have been built in one pharaoh's lifetime. Yet scholars think they were built over mere decades for three pharaohs who were father, son, and grandson (Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure). Egyptologists Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass have been trying to solve the puzzle of where the 20,000 or 30,000 laborers who are thought to have built the Pyramids lived. Ultimately, they hope to learn more about the workforce, their daily lives, and perhaps where they came from. In the meantime, Lehner has been excavating the bakeries that presumably fed this army of workers, while Hawass has been unearthing the cemetery for this grand labor force. The two scholars believe that Giza housed a skeleton crew of workers who labored on the Pyramids year-round. But during the late summer and early autumn months, when the Nile flooded surrounding fields, a large labor force would appear at Giza to put in time on the Pyramids. passages.text: The three famous Pyramids of Giza were built by three pharaohs that succeeded each other: Pharaohs Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure. Khafre was the son of Khufu, and Menkaure was the son of Khafre, so technically the three Pyramids of Giza were built by three generations of the same family as their tombs. Of course, the pharaohs did not build the pyramids by themselves, so read on to find out more about who was in charge of the construction, and who the people were that actually put all of the stones together to form these magnificent monuments. Khufu's Pyramid Was Built by Khufu in The Old Kingdom Khufu's Pyramid, also known as the Great Pyramid of Giza because it is the largest of the three pyramids on the site, was built by Khufu, who was the son of Sneferu, the founding pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty of Egypt during the Old Kingdom. It is likely that these two pyramids were also built by their pharaoh's viziers, in a similar manner to which the pyramid of Khufu was built. A little less is known about this, however, with more information being available on Hemiunu, Khufu's vizier, because more archaeological evidence was found in his tomb, including a statue of him. The real achievement was not lifting the stones, but organization: feeding, housing, assigning, and keeping tens of thousands of people motivated over decades, in a state without money, without literacy in the modern sense, and without any precedent. This page goes through step by step who was involved: the king who ordered it, the man who led it, and the people who did it. The Client and the Builder Are Not the Same First, a distinction that is constantly blurred in both German and English: the client and the builder are not the same. Who commissioned the Great Pyramid is a question about the king. The answer is Khufu, the second ruler of the 4th Dynasty, in Greek form Cheops. He ordered the construction, financed it, and had it built for himself. He built nothing himself. The same applies to his son Khafre and his successor Menkaure regarding the other two complexes. This separation is more than semantics because it explains why the monuments are named as they are. A pyramid bears the name of the person to be buried in it, not the name of its constructor.

The short answer is: Egyptians. Paid, fed, medically cared for, and organized into named crews, with an administration above them and a named chief architect at the top. If you ask which civilization built the Pyramids of Giza, you get an unusually well-documented answer. For hardly any other ancient mega-project do we know so much about the people who worked there. We know their housing, their bakeries, their graves, their broken bones, the names of their squads, and in one case even the service record of a mid-level official with delivery dates. The Great Pyramid was built by quarrying an estimated 2.3 million large blocks, weighing 6 million tonnes in total. The majority of the stones are not uniform in size or shape, and are only roughly dressed.[6] The outside layers were bound together by mortar, primarily local limestone from the Giza Plateau was used for its construction. Other blocks were imported by boat on the Nile: white limestone from Tura for the casing, and blocks of granite from Aswan, weighing up to 80 tonnes, for the "King's Chamber" structure.[7] There are three known chambers inside of the Great Pyramid.
